paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate a high-dimensional average when some observations have been maliciously corrupted. Its setting has two important structural assumptions: the clean observations follow a Gaussian distribution with identity covariance, and the unknown mean has only k nonzero coordinates. The goal is to use that sparsity while remaining robust to adversarial outliers.

Previous algorithms already needed relatively few samples, with requirements polynomial in sparsity, the logarithm of dimension, and inverse contamination fraction. Their computational cost, however, included a quadratic dependence on dimension. The abstract identifies the sample covariance matrix as the source of this obstacle: it contains a number of entries proportional to the square of the dimension.

The contribution is an algorithm with subquadratic runtime that retains the stated polynomial sample requirement. It builds on advances in detecting weak correlations. This separates the computational burden from explicitly handling a full covariance matrix, addressing a bottleneck that can make robust estimation expensive in high dimensions.
icml-2024-a-subquadratic-time-algorithm-.tldr: A new algorithm breaks the quadratic runtime barrier for robust sparse mean estimation under a Gaussian model while retaining polynomial sample requirements.

paragraphs: This paper studies choosing actions in offline linear bandits, where decisions must be made using already available information. Its objective is Bayesian regret: the expected loss from choosing an action instead of the best one, accounting for uncertainty. The authors question a common prescription that selects whichever action has the largest lower confidence bound on reward.

They propose optimizing a quantity directly tied to the desired objective. Their algorithm minimizes upper bounds on Bayesian regret using efficient conic optimization solvers. The derivation connects these regret bounds to monetary risk measures, bringing tools for reasoning about uncertain financial outcomes into the analysis of uncertain action rewards.

A matching lower bound establishes tightness of the proposed upper bounds. The authors use this result to guarantee an advantage over the lower-confidence-bound approach in their setting. Numerical experiments on synthetic domains also favor the proposed method. Together, the theoretical and numerical findings support targeting Bayesian regret directly when choosing actions in this offline problem.
icml-2024-bayesian-regret-minimization-i.tldr: Directly optimizing tight Bayesian regret bounds provides a theoretically supported alternative to lower-confidence-bound action selection in offline linear bandits.

paragraphs: Block gradient descent updates one group of variables while holding the others fixed. Although it can work well empirically, conventional choices of step size have not explained its advantage over ordinary gradient descent in deterministic convergence analyses. This paper asks whether choosing better step sizes can reveal an acceleration mechanism within the block updates themselves.

The authors examine least-squares problems with two variable blocks, assuming that the data matrix associated with each block is orthogonal. Within this setting, they derive optimal step sizes in closed form. Their proof minimizes the spectral radius of a matrix governing convergence, thereby choosing steps according to the behavior of the overall iteration.

Under the orthogonality assumption, the resulting asymptotic convergence rates are twice as fast as those of gradient descent with Polyak momentum, despite adding no momentum to the block method. The step sizes also improve a previous convergence rate for generalized alternating projection between two subspaces. The acceleration claim is therefore tied to a specific, explicitly analyzed structure.
icml-2024-block-acceleration-without-mom.tldr: For two-block least-squares problems with orthogonal block matrices, optimized step sizes accelerate block gradient descent without momentum.

paragraphs: Synthetic data can make information useful beyond the organizations holding the original records. However, generating it often assumes that a trusted central party can collect raw data for model training. CaPS addresses situations where distributed data holders cannot or do not want to give such a party access to their records.

The framework combines two privacy mechanisms with distinct roles. Secure multi-party computation replaces the trusted aggregator, providing input privacy during the collaborative computation. Differential privacy provides output privacy for the resulting synthetic data. This distinction matters because protecting the data used during training and protecting what a released dataset reveals are separate requirements.

CaPS applies generally to marginal-based synthetic tabular data generation, which uses summaries of selected combinations of variables. The authors demonstrate its applicability and scalability with MWEM+PGM and AIM, two select-measure-generate algorithms. The contribution is a way to carry out this family of methods collaboratively while incorporating privacy protections at both the computation and release stages.
icml-2024-caps-collaborative-and-private.tldr: CaPS combines secure multi-party computation and differential privacy to generate synthetic tabular data collaboratively without a trusted raw-data aggregator.

paragraphs: An object may be represented through three or more views or modalities. Learning their shared meaning often relies on objectives designed for pairs, either comparing every pair separately or comparing one view with an average of the others. This paper introduces a loss that treats all views jointly, preserving their role in a complete group.

The multi-marginal matching gap compares two costs within a batch. One measures the known groups of embeddings belonging to the same objects. The other finds an optimal arrangement of groups using multi-marginal optimal transport. Contrasting these costs gives the model a training signal based on how the true groupings compare with alternative joint matchings.

The underlying transport problem has exponential complexity in the number of views. Nevertheless, experiments show that a generalized Sinkhorn algorithm can handle three to six views with batches of roughly 64 to 128 examples. The reported results improve on multiview extensions of pairwise losses in both self-supervised and multimodal tasks, supporting the practical value of joint comparisons at these scales.
icml-2024-contrasting-multiple-represent.tldr: M3G learns from multiple views jointly through an optimal-transport matching loss, improving on pairwise-loss extensions in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: When training data contain different groups or domains, changes in their distribution can cause large performance drops. One response is to optimize performance on the worst-performing group. The paper highlights a tradeoff in that strategy: improving the worst group can come at the expense of performance on other groups.

The authors introduce an optimization scheme intended to find a good balance across groups without severely sacrificing any one of them. Applying this scheme to every network parameter would be computationally expensive and difficult. Controllable Prompt Tuning combines the scheme with prompt tuning, concentrating adaptation in a small set of tunable parameters.

On benchmarks involving spurious correlations, the procedures achieve reported state-of-the-art results while tuning only 0.4% of parameters. The evaluations cover transformer and non-transformer architectures, as well as unimodal and multimodal data. These findings support prompt tuning as an efficient vehicle for the proposed group-balancing objective, with demonstrated applicability across several model and data types.
icml-2024-controllable-prompt-tuning-for.tldr: Controllable Prompt Tuning balances performance across groups while adapting only 0.4% of parameters in the reported robustness experiments.

paragraphs: X-MDPT generates person images guided by a target pose and information from a reference image. It uses a masked diffusion transformer operating on latent patches, replacing the commonly used U-Net architecture. Working with these patches provides the foundation for a model whose image quality improves as its size increases in the reported evaluations.

The design combines three components. A diffusion transformer performs denoising, an aggregation network combines conditioning information into one vector, and a masked cross-prediction module strengthens representations using semantic information from the reference image. Together, these components connect the generation process with the conditions specifying the desired person image.

On DeepFashion, the authors report state-of-the-art performance and efficiency gains. Their compact 33 MB model achieves FID 7.42 versus 8.07 for a prior latent U-Net diffusion approach, using one-eleventh as many parameters. Their best model also surpasses a pixel-based diffusion approach with two-thirds as many parameters and 5.43 times faster inference. Larger variants improve FID, SSIM, and LPIPS.
icml-2024-cross-view-masked-diffusion-tr.tldr: X-MDPT uses masked diffusion transformers to improve pose-guided person generation, with reported gains in image quality and efficiency on DeepFashion.

paragraphs: In multi-agent reinforcement learning, agents interact in ways that can affect one another's outcomes. This paper asks how to quantify that influence rather than simply observe that interactions exist. It introduces total and state influence measurement functions intended to express dependencies across common multi-agent settings, including discounted rewards.

For the average-reward setting, the authors define total impact measurement and state impact measurement. These quantities describe influence through the maximum effect one agent can have on another agent's expected return. The paper also develops algorithms that approximate these quantities while learning approximations of the agents' expected returns.

The analysis supplies error bounds, convergence guarantees, and results on stability when policies change. Apart from observing other agents' actions, the approximation algorithm is decentralized. Empirical studies show that it can identify intricate influence structures in complex interactions. The contribution combines a way to define influence with a way to estimate it and theoretical support for those estimates in the average-reward setting.
icml-2024-detecting-influence-structures.tldr: The paper defines and estimates agents' influence on one another's returns, with decentralized algorithms and convergence guarantees for the average-reward setting.

paragraphs: Many methods for generalizing beyond the training distribution rely on environment labels that identify different conditions within a dataset. Obtaining these labels can be expensive and shaped by annotator bias. Existing automatic discovery methods can also create a circular dependency: tuning their settings requires validation data with the environment labels they aim to discover.

Cross-Risk Minimization addresses this problem with two networks trained on separate random halves of the training data. Each network imitates confident mistakes its sibling makes on held-out examples. This unusual use of errors forms the basis of the environment-discovery procedure, which also supplies a recipe for hyperparameter tuning and avoids early stopping.

XRM can assign discovered environments to both training and validation data. The authors report that downstream algorithms using these environments achieve oracle worst-group accuracy. That finding supports the usefulness of the discovered divisions for robust learning: they enable performance on the weakest group comparable to the oracle result reported in the study.
icml-2024-discovering-environments-with-.tldr: XRM discovers environments through twin networks that learn from each other's confident mistakes, supporting robust learning without human-labeled environments for tuning.

paragraphs: Document-based visual question answering models answer questions about documents supplied as images. This paper shows that their answers can sometimes come from memorized training responses even after the relevant visual information has been removed. A correct-looking answer can therefore reveal retained training information rather than information visible in the supplied document.

The authors demonstrate extraction of personally identifiable information, including information that appeared only once in the training set. They quantify extractability in controlled experiments and distinguish cases attributable to generalization from those attributable to memorization. They also investigate factors affecting memorization across multiple state-of-the-art models.

The study proposes a heuristic countermeasure that empirically prevents extraction of personally identifiable information in the evaluated setting. This is an experimental finding about the countermeasure, rather than a universal privacy guarantee. The main contribution is to expose and measure a concrete privacy risk in document question answering while showing that an intervention can prevent the observed extraction behavior.
icml-2024-extracting-training-data-from-.tldr: Document question-answering models can reveal memorized personal information after visual evidence is removed, and a proposed heuristic prevents extraction in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains models collaboratively across data owners whose datasets may differ substantially. This paper focuses on calibration: whether a model's confidence corresponds to how often its predictions are correct. Improving prediction accuracy alone does not resolve this issue, and the authors find that existing aggregation approaches produce suboptimal calibration.

Their theoretical analysis shows a persistent lower bound on global calibration error even when variation in clients' label distributions is constrained. FedCal addresses calibration at both levels of the system. Each client uses a specific scaler to correct output misalignment without sacrificing prediction accuracy, and the scaler parameters are averaged to create a global scaler.

This design connects local confidence correction with a shared correction for the global model. In extensive experiments, FedCal reduces global calibration error by 47.66% on average compared with the best-performing baseline. The result supports treating confidence calibration as a distinct federated learning objective and coordinating its treatment across clients and the aggregated model.
icml-2024-fedcal-achieving-local-and-glo.tldr: FedCal averages client-specific calibration scalers to improve local and global confidence calibration, reducing global error by 47.66% on average in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Federated continual learning combines two sources of change: different clients hold different data, and each client learns tasks over time. Existing methods primarily try to keep tasks from interfering with one another. This paper emphasizes another opportunity: knowledge learned by one client on an earlier task may help a different client with another task.

The proposed algorithm, Powder, uses prompts to carry this knowledge between sequential tasks and across clients. It introduces a prompt generation and aggregation approach designed to support that transfer while reducing communication overhead and addressing privacy concerns. Prompts therefore serve as the representation through which the method organizes shared task knowledge.

The reported experiments show improved knowledge transfer and reduced communication costs. These findings support making positive transfer an explicit goal alongside managing interference in federated continual learning. The privacy component is described as a design intention to alleviate concerns; the abstract's stated experimental findings specifically concern communication savings and improved transfer.
icml-2024-federated-continual-learning-v.tldr: Powder transfers knowledge through prompts across clients and sequential tasks, improving transfer and reducing communication costs in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Pretrained diffusion models can help reconstruct signals from noisy linear measurements without being retrained for each inverse problem. This paper examines an approximation underlying recent methods: they use a Gaussian denoising posterior with a hand-designed isotropic covariance to estimate a conditional posterior mean. That covariance describes uncertainty in an overly uniform way.

The authors replace this handcrafted choice with covariance determined through maximum likelihood estimation. They develop plug-and-play approaches for pretrained models both with and without reverse covariance, allowing posterior covariance optimization without retraining. They also propose a scalable method that learns to predict posterior covariance using a representation built from an orthonormal basis.

The experiments show significant reconstruction improvements without requiring hyperparameter tuning. The central finding is that the uncertainty approximation is a useful point of intervention when adapting diffusion models to inverse problems. Improving covariance can strengthen reconstruction while retaining the ability to reuse pretrained models, and the separate learned representation addresses scalability of covariance prediction.
icml-2024-improving-diffusion-models-for.tldr: Principled posterior covariance estimates improve diffusion-based reconstruction from noisy linear measurements without requiring hyperparameter tuning in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper connects diffusion sampling with optimization through a geometric interpretation of denoising. Under the manifold hypothesis, adding random noise approximately moves data in directions orthogonal to the space where clean data lie. Removing that noise can therefore be understood as approximately projecting a point back toward the clean-data space.

Using this connection, the authors interpret denoising diffusion models as approximate gradient descent on a Euclidean distance function. They then analyze convergence of the DDIM sampler under assumptions about the denoiser's projection error. The interpretation retains its approximate character: the analysis explicitly accounts for errors in the learned projection.

The theory motivates a new gradient-estimation sampler that generalizes DDIM. With as few as five to ten function evaluations, it achieves reported state-of-the-art FID scores on pretrained CIFAR-10 and CelebA models. It also produces high-quality samples with latent diffusion models. These results show how an optimization-based account of denoising can guide a practical sampler requiring few model evaluations.
icml-2024-interpreting-and-improving-dif.tldr: An approximate projection view of denoising yields DDIM convergence analysis and a new sampler with strong reported results using five to ten evaluations.

paragraphs: Mechanistic Neural Networks incorporate governing differential equations into the representations learned by a neural network. The proposed Mechanistic Block can be inserted into standard architectures so that learning explicitly captures the dynamics underlying scientific data. This gives the representation a mathematical form that supports interpretation as well as prediction and modeling.

The computational core is NeuRLP, a relaxed linear programming solver inspired by a technique for expressing the solution of linear ordinary differential equations as a linear program. The authors design it to integrate with neural networks and enable scalable parallel processing on GPUs. This solver is central to making the equation-based block computationally practical.

The paper demonstrates applications ranging from discovering equations to modeling dynamical systems and reports significant performance relative to specialized state-of-the-art methods. Its contribution brings together a scientific representation and a compatible computational mechanism. The stated findings support the versatility of learning with explicit differential equations across the scientific applications examined.
icml-2024-mechanistic-neural-networks-fo.tldr: Mechanistic Neural Networks learn differential-equation representations through a GPU-parallelizable solver, supporting interpretable scientific modeling and equation discovery.

paragraphs: Neural radiance fields represent detailed three-dimensional scenes, and feature grids can improve their rendering speed and quality. Those grids also require substantial storage. This paper targets that storage burden by applying neural compression to the feature grids of an individual grid-based NeRF model.

The method uses nonlinear transform coding but avoids requiring a trained encoder. Because training data containing many independent scenes are unavailable, it optimizes compression end to end for each scene and uses lightweight decoders. This makes the individual scene the unit of optimization instead of depending on a large collection of scenes for learning an encoder.

The compression objective weights the tradeoff between storage rate and reconstruction distortion by importance. A sparse entropy model with masking also accounts for spatial differences within the latent feature grids. Experiments report better compression efficacy and reconstruction quality than existing approaches. The results support adapting both the objective and the coding model to the uneven spatial structure of NeRF features.
icml-2024-neural-nerf-compression-d20556.tldr: Scene-specific neural compression reduces NeRF feature-grid storage while improving reported compression efficacy and reconstruction quality.

paragraphs: Many sampling problems specify a probability density only up to an unknown normalizing constant. This paper develops a diffusion-based method for both drawing samples from such densities and estimating those constants. It adapts the idea of transporting a target distribution toward a Gaussian and then approximating the diffusion process in reverse.

The proposed Particle Denoising Diffusion Sampler simulates the reversed process with an iterative particle scheme. It also introduces a score-matching loss for that scheme. These components distinguish its sampling procedure from standard denoising diffusion models while retaining the overall strategy of using diffusion and reversal to reach a target distribution.

Under mild assumptions, PDDS provides asymptotically consistent estimates, meaning its estimates approach the correct quantities in the relevant limiting regime. The authors demonstrate the method on multimodal and high-dimensional sampling tasks. Its contribution therefore combines a sampling construction with a statistical guarantee, addressing both practical distributional challenges and the reliability of estimates as the asymptotic conditions are approached.
icml-2024-particle-denoising-diffusion-s.tldr: PDDS uses an iterative particle-based diffusion scheme to sample unnormalized densities and estimate normalizing constants consistently under mild assumptions.

paragraphs: Prompting and prefix tuning change how a pretrained transformer behaves through its supplied context. This paper asks a theoretical expressiveness question: can such changes make a pretrained model approximate arbitrary sequence-to-sequence functions? The authors establish affirmative universal-approximation results and show that smaller models than previously thought can have this capacity.

One result shows that prefix tuning a single attention head is sufficient to approximate any continuous function. Another shows that prefixing a transformer whose depth grows linearly with sequence length can approximate any sequence-to-sequence function. These are sufficiency results about model capacity under the paper's constructions, rather than claims that every pretrained transformer automatically has these properties.

The analysis also goes beyond establishing that an approximation exists. It gives Jackson-type bounds relating the necessary prefix length to a desired approximation precision. This adds a quantitative resource question to the expressiveness result: how long a prefix is needed to reach a given accuracy. Together, the results clarify the theoretical power of prefix-based adaptation.
icml-2024-prompting-a-pretrained-transfo.tldr: The paper proves universal-approximation results for prefix-tuned attention and transformers, including bounds on prefix length for a desired precision.

paragraphs: Pufferfish privacy allows privacy requirements to specify arbitrary secrets and an adversary's prior knowledge about data. That flexibility creates difficulties in designing tractable mechanisms with good utility. It also lacks the composition guarantees needed to apply it directly to iterative machine learning, where many successive computations must be accounted for.

The authors introduce a version based on Rényi divergence. Within this framework, they extend the Wasserstein mechanism to a broad range of noise distributions and provide ways to improve utility. This expands the available choices for adding privacy-preserving noise while working within a framework that explicitly models secrets and prior knowledge.

For iterative algorithms, the paper proves privacy amplification results under contractive noisy iterations, offering an alternative to composition. It also demonstrates an application to private convex optimization. Shift reduction lemmas, including extensions developed in the paper, support both sets of results. The iteration guarantee depends on the stated contractive structure, making that condition central to the proposed route into iterative learning.
icml-2024-renyi-pufferfish-privacy-gener.tldr: Rényi Pufferfish privacy broadens additive-noise mechanisms and provides privacy amplification guarantees for contractive noisy iterations.

paragraphs: Decentralized partially observable decision problems involve multiple players acting with incomplete information. Earlier theory transforms such a problem into an equivalent single-player game and applies Bellman's principle to split it into stages. However, each stage still couples all players' decision variables, leaving the resulting backup operations with double-exponential complexity.

This paper shows how hierarchical information sharing permits a further decomposition while preserving optimality. The authors apply the principle of optimality again within each single-stage subgame, dividing it into smaller subgames. This makes it possible to handle one player's decision at a time instead of solving all coupled decisions together.

The analysis establishes extensive-form game representations with solutions to the single-stage subgames and substantially reduces time complexity. Experiments show that algorithms using these findings scale to much larger multiplayer games without giving up optimality. Hierarchical information sharing is the structural condition enabling this result; the contribution shows how that information organization can be used computationally in exact planning.
icml-2024-solving-hierarchical-informati.tldr: Under hierarchical information sharing, decomposing joint decision stages into smaller games enables more scalable planning while preserving optimality.

paragraphs: VoxBind generates three-dimensional molecules conditioned on protein structures. It represents molecules as grids of atomic density and learns with a three-dimensional voxel-denoising network. This connects the generation process directly to a spatial representation of molecules and the protein structures that guide their design.

The method extends neural empirical Bayes to conditional generation and separates generation into two steps. First, underdamped Langevin sampling uses a learned score function to draw noisy molecules from a Gaussian-smoothed conditional distribution. Second, a single denoising step estimates clean molecules from those noisy samples. Sampling and cleaning therefore operate as distinct parts of the procedure.

Compared with the stated current state of the art, the authors report simpler training, significantly faster sampling, and better results on extensive computational benchmarks. The generated molecules are more diverse, have fewer steric clashes, and show higher binding affinity to protein pockets in those evaluations. These are in silico findings, supporting the approach's promise for structure-conditioned molecular generation within the tested computational setting.
icml-2024-structure-based-drug-design-by.tldr: VoxBind generates protein-conditioned molecules by sampling and denoising atomic-density grids, improving speed and molecular properties on computational benchmarks.

paragraphs: Predictions often guide the allocation of public goods and interventions, but their value comes from the outcomes they help produce. A social planner may also improve welfare by expanding access or making an intervention more effective. This paper asks how gains from better prediction compare with gains available through other policy choices.

Its main contribution is a theoretical comparison between improving predictions and expanding access. Within several statistical models commonly used in quantitative social science, the authors derive simple, sharp conditions determining their relative value. This frames predictive improvement as one option in a broader allocation problem, with its usefulness assessed through welfare.

The paper also illustrates how the theoretical insights can inform the design of algorithmic decision systems in practice. The findings do not establish a universal preference for better prediction or broader access; their comparisons depend on the conditions in the analyzed models. Their value is to make the choice explicit and mathematically assessable when the ultimate objective is improving social outcomes.
icml-2024-the-relative-value-of-predicti.tldr: The paper derives conditions for when better predictions improve welfare more or less than expanding access to goods or interventions.

paragraphs: Latent embeddings represent complex objects as vectors, but the original objects may support operations with mathematical rules. Sets, for example, can be combined by union, and union obeys associativity. The paper asks how an operation performed on embeddings can respect these rules rather than merely approximate individual examples of the operation.

The proposed procedure learns a bijection between latent space and a carefully constructed mirrored algebra on Euclidean space. Operations are carried through this mapping, using the algebra's designed rules. The resulting parameterization is provably consistent with the desired laws, making structural consistency part of how the operation is built.

The authors evaluate these structural transport networks across several mirrored algebras against methods that operate directly in latent space. Their experiments provide strong evidence that respecting the input objects' algebraic structure helps learn accurate and self-consistent operations. The theoretical guarantee concerns the laws, while the experiments assess how this structured construction performs when learning the operations.
icml-2024-transport-of-algebraic-structu.tldr: Structural transport networks build latent operations that provably respect algebraic laws and show improved accuracy and consistency in experiments.

paragraphs: Pixel-level text-processing tasks often use separate architectures, training strategies, and formulations. That fragmentation makes systems harder to research, maintain, and deploy. UPOCR combines diverse tasks into a single image-to-image framework, so the model receives an image and produces the image-form output appropriate to the requested task.

The architecture uses a vision-transformer encoder and decoder with learnable task prompts. The encoder extracts general features, and the prompts steer those features toward task-specific representations so the decoder knows which operation to perform. Training uses a shared objective that minimizes differences between predicted images and their ground-truth targets across tasks.

The authors evaluate text removal, text segmentation, and tampered-text detection. They report that one unified model simultaneously achieves state-of-the-art performance on all three tasks. The finding supports a shared design for these pixel-level OCR applications: common representations and a common training objective can work together with task prompts to produce different kinds of outputs.
icml-2024-upocr-towards-unified-pixel-le.tldr: UPOCR unifies text removal, segmentation, and tampering detection in one prompted image-to-image model with reported state-of-the-art performance on all three.

paragraphs: This paper asks when knowledge learned in one problem can make learning another problem more efficient. It introduces a framework covering supervised, reinforcement, and imitation learning. Environments arise from a shared structural causal model, with its parameters chosen from restricted sets that describe what can vary across problems.

The authors derive a procedure that propagates parameter restrictions through the causal graph to other parameters being learned. Those derived restrictions can narrow the learning problem and enable transfer. The framework therefore links transfer opportunities to how known constraints interact with the model's causal structure.

The analysis shows that sparse changes between environments are neither necessary nor sufficient for transfer. It also gives an example where freezing an entire neural-network layer leads to poor transfer performance. Using the proposed procedure to choose a more refined set of parameters to freeze makes transfer successful in that example. These results challenge broad heuristics by showing why the structure of parameter relationships matters.
icml-2024-when-is-transfer-learning-poss.tldr: A causal framework identifies transfer opportunities through parameter restrictions and shows that sparse changes alone neither guarantee nor are required for transfer.
